experiment.rationale: This design exploits the core structural difference between Take-The-Best (TTB) and Tallying: TTB's choice (and its predicted choice probability, sigmoid(beta)) is determined solely by the single highest-validity discriminating cue and is therefore INVARIANT to how many lower-validity cues oppose it, whereas Tallying's predicted probability is a softmax over win counts and is therefore GRADED in the tally margin. I use 5 features with a wide, strictly ordered validity spread [0.95, 0.85, 0.75, 0.65, 0.55] so the cue hierarchy is unambiguous. The critical trials (T1-T4 and their mirrors T5-T8) hold the TTB-relevant structure fixed — the top cue (validity 0.95) always discriminates in favor of the same option — while the tally margin against that option grows from 0 (tie) to 1, 2, and 3. TTB predicts a FLAT probability of choosing the top-cue winner across all four margin levels (identical sigmoid(beta) - epsilon mixture), while Tallying predicts a monotonically DECLINING curve: 0.5, sigmoid(-beta), sigmoid(-2beta), sigmoid(-3beta). This is a quantitative, parametric signature: the slope of P(top-cue winner) vs. tally margin is exactly zero under TTB and strongly negative under Tallying. Trials T9-T12 repeat the same logic with the top cue tied and the second cue (0.85) discriminating, and T15-T16 with the third cue (0.75) discriminating, testing whether the dissociation persists deeper in the cue hierarchy (TTB predicts the same flat sigmoid(beta) at every cue level; Tallying's predictions depend only on counts, not on which cue discriminates). Trials T13-T14 are agreement trials (both heuristics favor the same option) serving as a baseline. Every conflict type appears in both A-favored and B-favored versions to absorb side/position bias. With 16 unique pairs, K = 96 // 16 = 6 repetitions yields exactly 96 trials per subject. Predicted dissociation summary: (1) on tally-tie trials with a discriminating top cue (T1, T5, T9, T11), TTB predicts above-chance preference for the cue winner while Tallying predicts exactly 50/50 regardless of beta; (2) across the margin gradient (T1->T4), TTB predicts zero slope, Tallying predicts a steep negative slope; (3) TTB is indifferent to which cue in the hierarchy discriminates (same probability at f0, f1, f2 levels for matched tally structure), while any validity-sensitive weighting would break this invariance.

metric.rationale: This metric is the proportion of trials on which subjects choose TAKE-THE-BEST's favored option, restricted to the 'pure conflict' trials where the two heuristics disagree (the tally majority favors the opposite option to the top discriminating cue). In this design those are trials T2,T3,T4,T6,T7,T8,T10,T12,T15,T16 — 10 of 16 trial types, i.e. 60 of the 96 trials per subject, so the per-subject estimate is based on a large sample and is very stable. Predicted values: under TTB, every conflict trial has identical choice probability p = (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta) + eps/2 > 0.5 for any beta>0, eps<0.5 (e.g. ~0.73 at beta=1, ~0.87 averaged over the parameter prior, approaching 1 at large beta). Under Tallying, the same trials have probability (1-eps)*sigmoid(-m*beta)+eps/2 with tally margins against the TTB option of 1, 2, or 3, which is strictly BELOW 0.5 for any beta>0 (e.g. ~0.17 at beta=1, ~0.13 averaged over the prior, approaching 0 at large beta). So the two theories sit on opposite sides of 0.5 with a large signed gap (~0.5-0.75) that persists across the whole plausible parameter range, while per-subject binomial variance is tiny (sd ~0.06-0.12 per subject with 60 conflict trials). I deliberately excluded tie trials (where Tallying guesses at exactly 0.5) and agreement trials, because including them only dilutes the mean gap without reducing variance enough to compensate. The metric is a simple proportion, so it is well-defined both on the pooled DataFrame and on each single subject's slice, and it involves no free parameters, no fitting, and no hashing of the list-valued rating columns.

proposer_theory.description: People compare two options by consulting cues one at a time in order of validity, stopping at the first cue that discriminates between the two options. That cue alone determines the choice: the option with the higher value on the discriminating cue wins, and no other cue is consulted. Cues with lower validity are never reached when a higher-validity cue already discriminates, so Take The Best is a "one-reason" decision rule — only a single feature is ever used on any given choice. Because only the sign of the comparison on the top discriminating cue matters, TTB ignores both the magnitude of that difference and all information on lower-validity cues, making it maximally frugal in the use of evidence. Cue validities are subjective and can be learned, inferred from instructions, or fixed by task structure. When no cue discriminates (all feature-wise comparisons tie) the learner has no basis for preference and must guess. Response noise enters through a softmax over the binary TTB score (winner = 1, loser = 0) with inverse temperature beta, plus an independent lapse that with probability epsilon replaces the softmax output with a uniform pick over the two options.
proposer_theory.predict_source:
def predict(parameters, stimulus, history):
    # Paper-faithful Take The Best (Gigerenzer & Goldstein 1996).
    # Stimulus is the pair of option feature vectors for the current
    # trial: array-like of shape (2, n_features), row 0 = option A,
    # row 1 = option B. Cue cascade: features are consulted in order
    # of descending validity; the first discriminating cue (strict
    # inequality) determines the winner; if no cue discriminates,
    # the model guesses uniformly. History is ignored.
    stim = np.asarray(stimulus, dtype=float)
    if stim.ndim != 2 or stim.shape[0] != 2:
        raise ValueError(
            f"TTB expects a (2, n_features) stimulus; got shape {stim.shape}."
        )
    n_features = stim.shape[1]

    val = np.asarray(parameters["validities"], dtype=float)
    if val.shape[0] != n_features:
        raise ValueError(
            f"validities length {val.shape[0]} != n_features {n_features}."
        )
    # Descending validity; argsort is stable so validity ties break
    # toward the earlier feature index.
    cue_order = np.argsort(-val, kind="stable").tolist()

    a, b = stim[0], stim[1]
    winner = None
    for j in cue_order:
        if a[j] > b[j]:
            winner = 0
            break
        if b[j] > a[j]:
            winner = 1
            break

    if winner is None:
        # No discriminating cue — pure guess.
        return np.ones(2) / 2.0

    scores = np.array([1.0, 0.0]) if winner == 0 else np.array([0.0, 1.0])

    beta = float(parameters["beta"])
    epsilon = float(parameters["epsilon"])

    # Softmax with max-subtraction for numerical stability. For the
    # binary TTB score this collapses to sigmoid(beta) for the winner,
    # giving a direct mapping from beta onto the paper's flip-noise
    # levels (beta=0 ↔ 50/50; beta ≫ 1 ↔ deterministic).
    z = beta * (scores - scores.max())
    e = np.exp(z)
    p_core = e / e.sum()

    n_opts = p_core.shape[0]
    return (1.0 - epsilon) * p_core + epsilon * (np.ones(n_opts) / n_opts)

experiment.rationale: This design's core novelty is a cue-allegiance flip at FIXED tally counts — the mirror image of the classic margin-gradient design. Tallying's predicted probability depends ONLY on the win counts through a softmax, which is shift-invariant (softmax over [3,2] equals softmax over [1,0]); it is therefore EXACTLY invariant to which features each option wins on and to cue depth. TTB's choice, in contrast, is determined solely by the allegiance of the highest-validity discriminating cue. The factorial core (trials 1-8) crosses tally margin {1, 2} x top-cue allegiance {pro-tally (agree), anti-tally (conflict)}: (i) C+ vs C- (and H+ vs H-) hold the win counts and even the tie placement identical (f0 tied, counts 3-2) while permuting cue allegiances so the top discriminating cue flips from favoring the tally winner to opposing it. Tallying predicts a precisely zero change in P(A) (identical sigma(beta)); TTB predicts a full flip from sigma(beta) to sigma(-beta). (ii) C vs H holds allegiance fixed and doubles the margin: TTB predicts exactly zero change (its probability is sigma(beta) for the top-cue winner regardless of how many cues oppose it), while Tallying predicts sigma(beta) -> sigma(2beta). The two theories thus occupy orthogonal cells of the 2x2: TTB shows a main effect of allegiance only; Tallying a main effect of margin only. The depth series (trials 9-14) places the anti-tally win at f0 (v=.95), f2 (v=.85), or f3 (v=.65), all at margin 1 with counts (3,2) or (2,1): both theories predict FLAT behavior here (TTB's probability is cue-depth invariant; Tallying's softmax is shift-invariant across (3,2)/(2,1)), so any validity-weighted hybrid would break this double invariance — a sharp signature that neither target theory but only mixtures would produce. The extreme anchors (trials 15-16) are 1-vs-5 splits where the top cue alone opposes five cues: TTB predicts P(cue winner) = sigma(beta) — numerically IDENTICAL to its prediction on the margin-1 conflict trials (invariance to 4 extra opposing cues), while Tallying predicts sigma(4beta) for the tally winner, near-deterministic at any reasonable beta. Quantitative dissociation summary: (1) on the allegiance flip (C+/C-, H+/H-), Tallying's predicted slope is exactly 0 and TTB's is -tanh(beta/2); (2) on the margin manipulation (C vs H), TTB's predicted slope is exactly 0 and Tallying's is positive; (3) across the depth series both are flat, jointly excluding weighted hybrids; (4) E1 vs C- isolates TTB's cue-count invariance against Tallying's steep margin gradient. Mirrors of every trial type absorb side/position bias. With 16 unique pairs, K = 96 // 16 = 6, yielding exactly 96 trials per subject.

def metric(data: pd.DataFrame) -> float:
    """Tally-vs-TTB choice-allegiance contrast.

    For every trial we determine (i) the TALLYING winner (option with more
    strict feature-wise wins) and (ii) the TAKE-THE-BEST winner (winner on
    the highest-validity discriminating cue, validities fixed by design as
    [0.95, 0.9, 0.85, 0.65, 0.6, 0.5]).  The metric is

        mean( response == tally winner ) - mean( response == TTB winner )

    On the 4 trial types where both heuristics pick the same option
    (trials 1, 3, 5, 7 and mirrors) the two indicators are identical and
    cancel.  On the 12 conflict trial types they are exact complements, so
    the metric reduces to 0.75 * (2*P(tally winner | conflict) - 1): strongly
    positive under Tallying, strongly negative under TTB.
    """
    validities = np.array([0.95, 0.9, 0.85, 0.65, 0.6, 0.5])
    cue_order = np.argsort(-validities, kind="stable")

    a_col = data["option_a_ratings"].tolist()
    b_col = data["option_b_ratings"].tolist()
    r_col = data["response"].tolist()

    tally_match = []
    ttb_match = []

    for ca, cb, cr in zip(a_col, b_col, r_col):
        a = np.asarray(ca, dtype=float).ravel()
        b = np.asarray(cb, dtype=float).ravel()
        r = int(cr)

        # Tallying winner: more strict feature-wise wins (ties on a feature
        # contribute to neither side).
        a_wins = float(np.sum(a > b))
        b_wins = float(np.sum(b > a))
        if a_wins > b_wins:
            tally_winner = 0
        elif b_wins > a_wins:
            tally_winner = 1
        else:
            tally_winner = -1  # undiscriminating tally -> excluded

        # TTB winner: first discriminating cue in descending-validity order.
        ttb_winner = -1
        for j in cue_order:
            if a[j] > b[j]:
                ttb_winner = 0
                break
            if b[j] > a[j]:
                ttb_winner = 1
                break

        if tally_winner >= 0:
            tally_match.append(1.0 if r == tally_winner else 0.0)
        if ttb_winner >= 0:
            ttb_match.append(1.0 if r == ttb_winner else 0.0)

    if len(tally_match) == 0 or len(ttb_match) == 0:
        return 0.0

    return float(np.mean(tally_match) - np.mean(ttb_match))
metric.rationale: The design's 16 trial types split into 4 agree types (tally winner = TTB winner: trials 1, 3, 5, 7) and 12 conflict types (tally winner = TTB loser: trials 2, 4, 6, 8-16). The metric is the difference between overall choice-consistency with Tallying and overall choice-consistency with TTB. On agree trials the two consistencies are identical and cancel; on conflict trials they are exact complements, so the metric equals 0.75 * (2*P(choose tally winner | conflict trials) - 1). Under simulated Tallying data, P(tally winner | conflict) = softmax over tallies (e.g. ~0.77 at beta=1, ~1.0 at large beta), giving a strongly POSITIVE value (~+0.4 at beta=1, up to +0.75). Under simulated TTB data, P(tally winner | conflict) = 1 - sigmoid(beta) (TTB always follows the top cue regardless of how many cues oppose it, including the 1-vs-5 anchors), giving a strongly NEGATIVE value (~-0.35 at beta=1, down to -0.75). The between-theory gap in the mean is therefore large at every plausible parameter setting (roughly 0.09 even at beta=0.1, ~0.27 at beta=0.3, ~0.75 at beta>=2), while per-subject variance stays tight because each subject contributes 96 trials (72 conflict) of simple binary indicators: per-subject SD ~0.08, so with N=25 subjects the Welch t-statistic ranges from ~4 (worst case, near-random parameters) to ~35 (moderate/large beta), comfortably below alpha=0.01. The metric works identically on the pooled DataFrame and on any single subject's slice (it is just a difference of two proportions), and it is side-balanced (the tally winner is option A on exactly 8 of the 16 trial types), so position/label bias cancels in expectation.

proposer_theory.description: People compare two options by counting, across all features, how often one option has a higher value than the other. The option that wins on more features is chosen. Tallying discards cardinal magnitudes — only the sign of each feature-wise comparison matters — so the heuristic is robust to monotone rescaling of individual features and cannot be swayed by a single large feature difference in the way Equal-Weight can. Ties on an individual feature contribute nothing to either count: that cue is simply treated as uninformative for the pair. No feature is privileged, in contrast to Take The Best; every cue contributes equally to the tally. When the two counts are equal the heuristic has no basis for preference and the learner must guess. Response noise enters through a softmax over the two tallies with inverse temperature beta (interpolating between fully deterministic choice at large beta and uniform guessing at beta = 0), plus an independent lapse that with probability epsilon replaces the softmax output with a uniform pick over the two options.

def predict(parameters, stimulus, history):
    # Paper-faithful Tallying heuristic (Dawes 1979; Gigerenzer &
    # Goldstein 1999). Stimulus is the pair of option feature vectors
    # for the current trial: array-like of shape (2, n_features),
    # with row 0 = option A, row 1 = option B. History is ignored.
    stim = np.asarray(stimulus, dtype=float)
    if stim.ndim != 2 or stim.shape[0] != 2:
        raise ValueError(
            f"Tallying expects a (2, n_features) stimulus; got shape {stim.shape}."
        )

    a, b = stim[0], stim[1]
    # Count strict feature-wise wins; ties contribute to neither option.
    a_wins = float(np.sum(a > b))
    b_wins = float(np.sum(b > a))
    scores = np.array([a_wins, b_wins])

    beta = float(parameters["beta"])
    epsilon = float(parameters["epsilon"])

    # Softmax with max-subtraction for numerical stability. When
    # a_wins == b_wins the softmax is exactly uniform regardless of
    # beta, which is the correct behavior for an undiscriminating
    # tally.
    z = beta * (scores - scores.max())
    e = np.exp(z)
    p_core = e / e.sum()

    n_opts = p_core.shape[0]
    return (1.0 - epsilon) * p_core + epsilon * (np.ones(n_opts) / n_opts)

next_theory.description: Noisy Validity-weighted evidence integration with capacity-interference and one-reason lapses (NVW). People do not use a single fixed heuristic; they pool all the expert ratings they can, but each cue's contribution is weighted by its validity raised to a steepness exponent gamma (gamma = 0 recovers Tallying, gamma -> infinity recovers Take-The-Best, so both classic heuristics are limiting cases). Integration is capacity-limited: beyond a working-memory span of about four cues, every additional cue that must be pooled multiplies the reliability (effective inverse temperature) of the integrated comparison by an interference factor delta < 1, so choice consistency is design-dependent and falls sharply as feature count grows. Each cue is additionally attended only with probability alpha (lapses of attention). On a minority of trials — with a probability omega that is modulated by how strongly the most valid discriminating cue's validity dominates the validity of the opposing side's cues — the agent abandons integration and makes a one-reason decision based solely on that top cue. The final choice is a softmax (at the capacity-scaled inverse temperature) over the attended, validity-weighted evidence difference, mixed with an independent lapse to uniform guessing.
next_theory.predict_source:
def predict(parameters, state, history):
    # NVW: Noisy Validity-weighted integration with capacity-interference
    # and one-reason lapses.
    # Stimulus: array of shape (2, n_features); row 0 = option A, row 1 = B.
    stim = np.asarray(state, dtype=float)
    if stim.ndim != 2 or stim.shape[0] != 2:
        raise ValueError(
            f"NVW expects a (2, n_features) stimulus; got shape {stim.shape}."
        )
    a, b = stim[0], stim[1]
    n = int(stim.shape[1])

    v = np.asarray(parameters["validities"], dtype=float).ravel()
    if v.shape[0] != n:
        raise ValueError(
            f"validities length {v.shape[0]} != n_features {n}."
        )

    gamma = float(parameters["gamma"])
    alpha = float(parameters["alpha"])
    beta = float(parameters["beta"])
    delta = float(parameters["delta"])
    epsilon = float(parameters["epsilon"])
    omega_base = float(parameters["omega_base"])
    omega_dom = float(parameters["omega_dom"])

    # (1) Validity-steepness weights: gamma = 0 -> Tallying (equal weights),
    # gamma -> infinity -> Take-The-Best (top cue only).
    w = np.power(v, gamma)

    # (3) Attention: each cue independently attended with probability alpha.
    att = np.random.random(n) < alpha
    a_win = (a > b) & att
    b_win = (b > a) & att
    disc = a_win | b_win

    # (3) Capacity / interference: beyond a working-memory span of ~4 cues,
    # each additional cue that must be pooled multiplies the reliability
    # (effective inverse temperature) of the integrated evidence by delta.
    # This makes decision noise grow with feature count.
    excess = max(0, n - 4)
    beta_eff = beta * (delta ** excess)

    def _sig(z):
        # Numerically stable logistic.
        return 0.5 * (1.0 + np.tanh(0.5 * np.asarray(z, dtype=float)))

    if not np.any(disc):
        # No attended discriminating cue: pure guess.
        p_a = 0.5
    else:
        # (1) Integration: softmax over the weighted evidence difference.
        d = float(np.sum(w[a_win]) - np.sum(w[b_win]))
        p_int = float(_sig(beta_eff * d))

        # (2) One-reason mode: the single most valid attended
        # discriminating cue decides (TTB-like), with confidence scaled
        # by that cue's weight and the effective sensitivity.
        idx = np.where(disc)[0]
        top = int(idx[np.argmax(v[idx])])
        s = 1.0 if a[top] > b[top] else -1.0
        p_1r = float(_sig(beta_eff * w[top] * s))

        # (2) Validity-dominance coupling for the one-reason lapse rate:
        # dominance of the top cue over the opposing side's cue validities.
        opp = b_win if s > 0 else a_win
        if np.any(opp):
            dom = float(v[top] - np.mean(v[opp]))
        else:
            dom = float(v[top] - 0.5)
        omega_t = float(np.clip(omega_base + omega_dom * dom, 0.0, 0.95))

        p_a = (1.0 - omega_t) * p_int + omega_t * p_1r

    probs = np.array([p_a, 1.0 - p_a], dtype=float)

    # (4) Independent lapse toward uniform guessing.
    probs = (1.0 - epsilon) * probs + epsilon * 0.5
    return probs
next_theory.rationale:
DIAGNOSIS OF PRIOR FAILURES. TTB (pi_1) predicts P(choose TTB winner | conflict) = 0.84 in Experiment 1 (real: 0.208) and a strongly negative tally-minus-TTB contrast of -0.48 in Experiment 2 (real: +0.158): it is far too one-reason driven. Tallying (pi_2) is almost right in Experiment 1 (0.136 vs 0.208, i.e. tally-consistency 0.86 vs real 0.79) but predicts the SAME invariant consistency in Experiment 2 (0.548 vs real 0.158, i.e. tally-consistency 0.86 vs real 0.605). The signature of the human data is therefore: (i) mostly integration, mildly validity-sensitive (slightly more TTB-leaning than pure tallying in Exp 1), and (ii) a large DROP in integration consistency when the cue set grows from 5 to 6 features. Crucially, I verified analytically that the two designs are matched on every conflict-trial statistic that a fixed-noise integrator sees (weighted margins, SNR, dominance of the top cue — if anything top-cue dominance is HIGHER in Exp 1), so no shared-parameter validity weighting alone can produce the gap; the gap must be carried by a feature-count-dependent noise term. This is exactly the arbiter's mechanism (3): 'effective decision noise grows with feature count'.

MECHANISMS. NVW implements the arbiter's prescription: (1) weights w_j = v_j^gamma nest Tallying (gamma=0) and TTB (gamma->inf); (2) a one-reason lapse mode with rate omega coupled to the validity dominance of the top discriminating cue over the opposing majority's cues; (3) cue-wise attention alpha plus a capacity/interference term: beyond a working-memory span of ~4 cues, each extra pooled cue multiplies evidence reliability by delta, so noise grows steeply with feature count; (4) softmax response rule with inverse temperature beta plus an independent lapse epsilon.

CALIBRATION LOGIC. Because parameters are sampled per subject from the declared ranges and metrics are computed on the pooled population, the ranges themselves are the population-level fit (this is visible in pi_2: its 0.86 tally-consistency in BOTH experiments equals 1 - E[epsilon]/2 under uniform sampling of epsilon in [0, 0.5]). I therefore derived the ranges analytically from the conflict-trial structure of both designs so that the SAME parameter distribution reproduces both targets: with gamma ~ U[0.7, 1.3], beta ~ U[5, 11], delta ~ U[0.18, 0.30], the effective Exp-1 sensitivity is beta*delta (mean ~1.9) and the effective Exp-2 sensitivity is beta*delta^2 (mean ~0.47). Averaging the logistic over these ranges yields Exp-1 tally-consistency ~0.79-0.80 (metric P(TTB winner|conflict) ~ 0.20-0.22, real 0.208) and Exp-2 tally-consistency ~0.60-0.61 (metric ~0.15-0.17, real 0.158). The one-reason lapse (omega ~ 0.02) and lapse (epsilon ~ 0.03) contribute the small residual top-cue choices without materially shifting the averages. This is why I propose tighter ranges than the arbiter's illustrative ones: under per-subject uniform sampling, wide ranges (e.g. gamma in [0,4]) would average TTB-like and tally-like subjects and destroy the fit; the ranges above are centered on the region that both experiments jointly identify.

DEVIATION FROM ARBITER DETAIL. I keep the validity-dominance coupling for omega but let its slope (omega_dom) be free-signed: computing actual dominance values (top-cue validity minus mean opposing validity) gives a HIGHER mean in Exp 1 (0.23) than Exp 2 (0.19), so an increasing-with-dominance coupling would push Experiment 1 toward TTB — the opposite of what the data show. The between-experiment gap is instead carried by the capacity-interference term, which is the arbiter's own mechanism (3). The coupling remains in the model, falsifiable against new designs that manipulate the validity gap at fixed tally margins.

FALSIFIABLE PREDICTIONS. NVW predicts (a) choice consistency falls sharply (geometrically) as feature count grows beyond ~4 at fixed tally margins — distinguishing it from Tallying's invariance; (b) deviations from tally invariance that grow with the validity spread of the cues (via gamma); (c) a small, validity-dominance-modulated minority of pure one-reason choices. It can be validated on new designs that independently manipulate feature count and the top-cue validity gap.

experiment.rationale: This design dissociates NVW (validity-weighted, capacity-limited integration with one-reason lapses) from Tallying by exploiting the fact that Tallying's predicted P(A) depends ONLY on the win-count margin: for any beta and epsilon, Tallying assigns exactly ONE probability to every trial with the same (a_wins, b_wins), and exactly 0.5 to every tie trial. NVW instead assigns a graded probability ordered by the validity-weighted evidence difference d = sum(v^gamma over A-won cues) - sum(v^gamma over B-won cues), plus a small one-reason tilt toward the highest-validity discriminating cue. I use n=5 (one cue beyond the working-memory span, so the interference factor delta is active but integration remains informative: beta_eff = beta*delta in [0.9, 3.3]) with a wide validity spread [0.95, 0.85, 0.75, 0.65, 0.55]. The design contains four dissociation axes, each with mirrored (A/B-swapped) versions to absorb side bias: (1) MARGIN-0 VALIDITY GRADIENT (types 1-5): 2-2 tie trials where the validity allocation varies from strongly pro-A (d=+0.60: A wins the two most valid cues) through d=+0.40, +0.20, 0.00, to a top-cue-conflict probe (d=+0.10 with the top cue favoring B). Tallying predicts EXACTLY 0.5 on all five types for every parameter value; NVW predicts a monotone deviation from 0.5 whose sign is parameter-free (because v^gamma preserves validity order for any gamma>0, A winning {f0,f1} vs B winning {f3,f4} yields d>0 at any gamma in [0.7,1.3]), with magnitude sigma(beta_eff*d) roughly 0.61-0.93 at d=0.60. (2) WITHIN-MARGIN-1 SPREAD (types 6-14): nine 3-2 trials spanning d from 1.35 down to 0.15. Tallying predicts an identical probability sigma(beta) on ALL nine; NVW predicts a monotone spread of at least ~0.12 (and up to ~0.5) across the aligned subseries (types 6-10, where the top cue also favors A, so both the integration and one-reason components agree). (3) ORDER REVERSAL: NVW predicts P(type 1; margin 0, d=0.60) > P(type 14; margin 1, d=0.15) strictly for every admissible parameter setting (the d-gap is positive at all gamma, and the one-reason lapse favors A on type 1 but B on type 14), whereas Tallying predicts the strict opposite ordering (0.5 < sigma(beta)). The sign of P(margin-0, high-d) - P(margin-1, low-d) is therefore a decisive, parameter-free test. (4) MATCHED-d ALLEGIANCE FLIP: types 9 vs 11 (both d=0.75) and 10 vs 12 (both d=0.55) hold counts AND the validity-weighted evidence identical while flipping which option wins the top cue; Tallying predicts exactly zero difference, NVW predicts a small positive difference (the one-reason lapse signature, magnitude up to ~0.07). Types 15-16 are margin-2 anchors probing the steepness of the margin gradient (Tallying: sigma(2beta); NVW: sigma(beta_eff*1.90) vs sigma(beta_eff*1.00), itself a within-margin spread Tallying cannot produce). In total Tallying predicts only THREE distinct choice probabilities across all 32 pairs (margin 0, 1, 2 and their complements), while NVW predicts a graded profile ordered by d with allegiance modulations - a sharp structural signature. With 32 unique pairs, K = 96 // 32 = 3, giving exactly 96 trials per subject.
